# CME Needs Assessment: Therapy-Induced Senescence in Glioblastoma and the Rationale for Adjuvant Senolytic Therapy

<!-- Generated by ChatGPT (chatgpt.com, Plus, "Medium" setting) from prompt_pack.md on 13 Oct 2026; copied verbatim from the chat. Only the section headings were re-marked as Markdown headings (lost when copying the rendered page). -->

Target audience: Neuro-oncologists, radiation oncologists, neurosurgeons, oncology pharmacists, and translational researchers.

## Background and burden

Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive primary brain malignancy characterized by frequent recurrence, treatment resistance, and poor survival despite surgical resection followed by radiotherapy and temozolomide (TMZ)-based chemotherapy. [PMID:33805316][PMID:37458855]

A review of residual disease in glioma reports median survival of less than two years after diagnosis, emphasizing the need for therapeutic strategies addressing residual treatment-resistant cells and tumor recurrence. [PMID:33805316]

Radiotherapy and TMZ induce cellular senescence, a stress-response program characterized by cell-cycle arrest that can initially suppress tumor proliferation. [PMID:37458855][PMID:39510171]

However, senescent glioblastoma cells can remain viable, develop a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), influence neighboring malignant and nonmalignant cells, and potentially escape senescence to resume proliferation. [PMID:37458855][PMID:40253386][PMID:41749804]

The SASP includes inflammatory cytokines, growth factors, and matrix-remodeling factors that can support tumor survival, invasion, stemness, and immune evasion within the glioblastoma microenvironment. [PMID:41749804][PMID:34580063]

Therapy-induced senescence also affects nonmalignant brain populations, including astrocytes, endothelial cells, and pericytes, potentially contributing to blood-brain barrier dysfunction, neurovascular injury, and cognitive impairment following cranial irradiation. [PMID:30615147][PMID:37642933][PMID:39110121]

Preclinical studies demonstrate that pharmacological or genetic clearance of senescent brain cells can mitigate radiation-associated neurovascular and cognitive dysfunction, supporting investigation of senescence-targeted interventions for both tumor control and treatment-related toxicity. [PMID:31960269][PMID:37642933][PMID:39513361]

Consequently, therapy-induced senescence represents a potential therapeutic target with implications for both glioblastoma recurrence and radiation-related neurological complications, although clinical translation remains investigational. [PMID:38030881][PMID:39510171]

## Current evidence

### 1. Mechanisms of therapy-induced senescence and tumor recurrence

Experimental studies have identified the p21-dependent DNA damage response as an important mediator of radiation-induced glioblastoma senescence. [PMID:39972068][PMID:40319068]

TMZ-induced senescence involves O6-methylguanine-associated DNA damage, mismatch repair-dependent activation of ATR/ATM-CHK1/CHK2-p53 signaling, and p21-mediated inhibition of CDK1/CDK2, resulting in G2-phase arrest. [PMID:40319068]

Nevertheless, TMZ-treated glioblastoma cells can escape senescence, reactivate proliferation, and acquire stem-like characteristics associated with enhanced colony formation, invasion, and chemotherapy resistance. [PMID:40253386]

HIF1α and HIF2α contribute to TMZ-associated senescence and subsequent stem-like reprogramming, while inhibition of these factors reduces senescent-cell and stem-like aggregate formation in experimental models. [PMID:40253386]

Studies of residual senescent glioblastoma cells also implicate the PERK–eIF2α–ATF4–CHOP unfolded protein response in senescence maintenance and reversal, with PERK inhibition exhibiting senolytic activity in residual senescent cells and preventing recurrence in an orthotopic mouse model. [PMID:39021199]

These findings support a model in which treatment-induced cell-cycle arrest may provide initial tumor suppression while persistent or escaping senescent cells subsequently contribute to tumor progression. [PMID:37458855][PMID:39021199][PMID:40253386]

### 2. Senescent astrocytes and the irradiated tumor microenvironment

In a 2021 preclinical investigation, cranial irradiation induced widespread senescence in mouse brains, particularly among astrocytes, and increased expression of p21 and SASP-associated factors, including hepatocyte growth factor (HGF). [PMID:34580063]

Senescent astrocytes promoted glioma migration and invasion through HGF-mediated activation of the Met receptor, while HGF-neutralizing antibodies and crizotinib inhibited these effects in experimental models. [PMID:34580063]

Administration of navitoclax (ABT-263) selectively eliminated senescent astrocytes and significantly attenuated glioma growth in preirradiated mouse brains. [PMID:34580063]

Subsequent research demonstrated that radiotherapy-induced astrocyte senescence promoted an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment through enhanced recruitment of myeloid inflammatory cells, while senolytic treatment after radiotherapy substantially prolonged survival in preclinical glioblastoma models. [PMID:38342629]

Additional mechanistic evidence identified astrocyte-derived IL-6 as a mediator of glioblastoma aggressiveness through JAK2/STAT3 activation, with ABT-263 and IL-6 receptor blockade suppressing tumor-promoting effects in experimental systems. [PMID:41385178]

Senescent astrocytes and pericytes have also been implicated in radiation-associated cognitive and vascular injury, suggesting that the biological consequences of senescence extend beyond the malignant compartment. [PMID:31960269][PMID:39110121]

### 3. Senescent glioblastoma cells as direct therapeutic targets

A 2025 study identified cellular inhibitor of apoptosis protein 2 (cIAP2), encoded by BIRC3, as a survival factor in radiation-induced senescent glioblastoma cells. [PMID:39972068]

Radiation-induced senescent glioblastoma cells increased BIRC3 expression and produced SASP factors, prominently IL-6, that activated JAK–STAT3 and NF-κB signaling in neighboring nonsenescent tumor cells. [PMID:39972068]

SMAC mimetics targeting cIAP2 induced apoptosis of senescent glioblastoma cells, and adjuvant birinapant administered after radiotherapy eliminated senescent tumor cells and prevented the emergence of recurrent tumors in patient-derived xenograft and immunocompetent mouse models. [PMID:39972068]

Other preclinical strategies have demonstrated senolytic activity through different mechanisms, including PERK inhibition, all-trans retinoic acid-mediated senescent astrocyte clearance, and clofoctol-associated apoptosis and ferroptosis in chemotherapy-induced senescent glioma cells. [PMID:39021199][PMID:39513361][PMID:42109835]

Clofoctol also synergized with TMZ and extended survival in glioblastoma mouse models. [PMID:42109835]

However, susceptibility to senolytic intervention is heterogeneous: TMZ pretreatment sensitized U87MG cells but not T98G cells to DR5-mediated apoptosis, and two of three primary patient-derived glioblastoma samples exhibited similar sensitization. [PMID:41249587]

### 4. Immune consequences and context-dependent effects

Chemotherapy-induced senescent glioblastoma cells have been shown to promote tumor-associated macrophage recruitment and M2-like polarization through a DDX58–STAT1–CSF1 signaling mechanism. [PMID:40259469]

Conversely, autophagy inhibition increased therapy-induced glioblastoma senescence while modifying the SASP to promote paracrine senescence, favor antitumor M1 macrophage polarization, and reduce recruitment of protumor neutrophils. [PMID:36472478]

These contrasting findings indicate that senescence-associated immune effects are context-dependent and that senescence induction cannot be assumed to be universally protumorigenic. [PMID:33378554][PMID:36472478][PMID:40259469]

### 5. Clinical translation, limitations, and safety

A phase 2 study of senolytics combined with anti-PD-1 therapy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma reported a 33.3% (95% confidence interval 16.6-54.7%) major pathological response rate and a 4.2% incidence of grade 3-4 adverse events; these findings provide clinical experience outside glioblastoma but do not establish benefit or safety in patients with glioblastoma. [PMID:40855191][NCT:NCT05724329]

An EARLY_PHASE1 study involving dasatinib, quercetin, fisetin, temozolomide, LMP744, and an autologous TLPO vaccine strategy is listed as RECRUITING for previously treated glioma with residual disease, with enrollment 30 and primary outcomes including completion of 3 cycles and turnaround time for scan and marker data. [NCT:NCT07025226]

The supplied evidence therefore supports clinical investigation of senolytic approaches but does not establish adjuvant senolysis as an evidence-based standard treatment for glioblastoma. [PMID:38030881][PMID:39510171][NCT:NCT07025226]

Safety and efficacy also require separate evaluation because the reported low incidence of severe adverse events in a non-GBM phase 2 study cannot establish the tolerability of different senolytic agents combined with glioblastoma radiochemotherapy. [PMID:40855191][PMID:38030881]

Furthermore, clearance of senescent cells does not uniformly improve disease outcomes: a study in an amyotrophic lateral sclerosis mouse model demonstrated reduced senescent-cell burden without significant improvement in motor function or survival. [PMID:41957276]

Timing may also influence treatment effects, as experimental clearance of p16-positive cells at 4 months after irradiation improved functional outcomes and median survival, whereas clearance at 1 month produced no corresponding benefit in a whole-body irradiation mouse model. [PMID:42649478]

## Practice gaps

The following practice gaps describe evidence-informed educational needs rather than documented population-level deficiencies in current clinician behavior.

Gap 1: Recognizing the dual biological consequences of therapy-induced senescence

What clinicians should do: Distinguish the initial tumor-suppressive effects of senescence from the potential long-term consequences of persistent SASP activity, senescence escape, and tumor microenvironment remodeling when interpreting therapeutic response and recurrence biology. [PMID:37458855][PMID:41749804]

What the evidence suggests happens: Experimental models demonstrate that glioblastoma cells can survive therapy in a senescent state, subsequently escape cell-cycle arrest, and acquire invasive, stem-like, or therapy-resistant characteristics. [PMID:40253386][PMID:39021199]

Educational need: Develop the ability to interpret senescence as a dynamic, context-dependent cellular state rather than an unequivocal marker of durable treatment success. [PMID:33378554][PMID:42546852]

Gap 2: Integrating tumor-cell and stromal senescence into recurrence models

What clinicians should do: Consider the contributions of both malignant and nonmalignant senescent cells when evaluating experimental explanations for glioblastoma recurrence after radiotherapy. [PMID:34580063][PMID:39972068]

What the evidence suggests happens: Studies identify complementary mechanisms involving senescent astrocyte-derived HGF–Met and IL-6–JAK2/STAT3 signaling, alongside tumor-cell-derived SASP activation of JAK–STAT3 and NF-κB pathways. [PMID:34580063][PMID:41385178][PMID:39972068]

Educational need: Recognize the distinct cellular sources and molecular mechanisms of the SASP and their potential implications for therapeutic target selection. [PMID:41749804][PMID:39972068]

Gap 3: Distinguishing senolytic preclinical efficacy from established clinical benefit

What clinicians should do: Critically appraise the experimental setting, target specificity, outcome measures, and clinical applicability of senolytic studies before interpreting them as evidence for patient treatment. [PMID:38030881][PMID:39510171]

What the evidence suggests happens: Multiple senolytic approaches have reduced tumor growth, delayed recurrence, or improved survival in glioblastoma mouse models, whereas the provided glioma trial record describes an early-phase recruiting study rather than completed efficacy results. [PMID:34580063][PMID:39972068][PMID:42109835][NCT:NCT07025226]

Educational need: Differentiate mechanistic proof of concept from clinical evidence sufficient to justify routine therapeutic adoption. [PMID:38030881][NCT:NCT07025226]

Gap 4: Evaluating patient selection and senolytic treatment timing

What clinicians should do: Recognize the potential importance of cellular heterogeneity, senescence biomarkers, and intervention timing when assessing investigational senolytic strategies. [PMID:41249587][PMID:41749804][PMID:42649478]

What the evidence suggests happens: TMZ-induced sensitivity to DR5-mediated apoptosis differs among glioblastoma models, while delayed senescent-cell clearance produced greater functional benefit than earlier clearance in an experimental irradiation model. [PMID:41249587][PMID:42649478]

Educational need: Identify why uniform senolytic treatment strategies may fail to account for differences in senescence induction, survival dependencies, and treatment-associated tissue responses. [PMID:41249587][PMID:42546852]

Gap 5: Balancing recurrence prevention against neurological and systemic outcomes

What clinicians should do: Evaluate proposed senolytic strategies using both antitumor and treatment-related toxicity outcomes, including neurological function and potential systemic effects. [PMID:31960269][PMID:41520729][PMID:38030881]

What the evidence suggests happens: Senescent-cell clearance improved neurovascular or cognitive outcomes in several irradiated mouse models, but ABT263 did not reverse irradiation-associated hepatic changes attributed to senescence-independent mechanisms in another animal study. [PMID:31960269][PMID:37642933][PMID:41520729]

Educational need: Recognize that successful senescent-cell elimination does not necessarily translate into uniform protection against all radiotherapy-associated complications. [PMID:41520729][PMID:41957276]

## Evidence gaps

1. Randomized glioblastoma efficacy evidence: The provided sources do not establish whether adjuvant senolytic therapy improves overall survival, progression-free survival, or recurrence outcomes in patients receiving standard radiotherapy and TMZ; the supplied glioma clinical trial record describes an EARLY_PHASE1 recruiting study without reported efficacy results. [PMID:38030881][NCT:NCT07025226]

2. Optimal senolytic selection: Comparative clinical evidence is insufficient to establish which investigational approach—such as BCL-2/BCL-xL inhibition, cIAP2 targeting, PERK inhibition, DR5 activation, or clofoctol-mediated senescent-cell elimination—offers the most favorable efficacy and safety profile in glioblastoma. [PMID:34580063][PMID:39972068][PMID:39021199][PMID:41249587][PMID:42109835]

3. Safety with glioblastoma radiochemotherapy: The supplied studies do not provide definitive clinical estimates of hematologic toxicity, neurological toxicity, drug interactions, or treatment discontinuation rates when senolytics are combined with radiotherapy and TMZ in glioblastoma patients. [PMID:38030881][PMID:39510171][NCT:NCT07025226]

4. Predictive biomarkers: Validated clinical biomarkers capable of distinguishing patients likely to benefit from senolysis are not established by the supplied evidence, despite experimental associations involving p21, BIRC3/cIAP2, DR5 sensitivity, and heterogeneous senescence-associated transcriptional states. [PMID:39972068][PMID:41249587][PMID:41749804][PMID:42546852]

5. Optimal sequencing and timing: The appropriate interval between radiotherapy, TMZ, and senolytic treatment remains unresolved, particularly given evidence that the timing of senescent-cell clearance can alter functional outcomes in irradiation models. [PMID:42649478][PMID:38030881]

6. Senescence detection in patients: The supplied literature does not establish a clinically validated, standardized assay for measuring senescent tumor and stromal populations during or after glioblastoma treatment, although single-cell and spatial profiling have been proposed as approaches for refining identification and patient selection. [PMID:41749804][PMID:42546852]

7. Long-term neurological outcomes: Whether senolytic treatment can sustainably improve cognition, preserve blood-brain barrier function, or reduce radiation-associated neurotoxicity in glioblastoma patients remains uncertain because the cited interventional evidence is predominantly preclinical. [PMID:31960269][PMID:37642933][PMID:39110121]

8. Context-dependent immune effects: Further research is needed to determine when therapy-induced senescence promotes immunosuppressive macrophage responses versus antitumor immune activity and how these differences should influence combination therapy development. [PMID:40259469][PMID:36472478]

9. Consequences of eliminating beneficial senescence: Clinical studies have not established how to selectively remove harmful senescent populations while preserving potentially beneficial tumor-suppressive senescence and tissue-homeostatic functions. [PMID:33378554][PMID:36472478][PMID:42546852]

## Proposed learning objectives

Upon completion of this activity, participants will be able to:

1. Differentiate the tumor-suppressive and tumor-promoting consequences of radiotherapy- and TMZ-induced senescence, including the roles of SASP signaling, senescence escape, and interactions between malignant and stromal populations. [PMID:37458855][PMID:40253386][PMID:41749804]

2. Evaluate the mechanistic rationale and preclinical efficacy of investigational senolytic strategies targeting BCL-2/BCL-xL, cIAP2, PERK, and other senescence-associated vulnerabilities in glioblastoma. [PMID:34580063][PMID:39972068][PMID:39021199][PMID:42109835]

3. Appraise the limitations of current senolytic evidence, including treatment timing, biomarker heterogeneity, safety, and the distinction between preclinical outcomes and clinical efficacy when considering future glioblastoma trials. [PMID:41249587][PMID:42649478][PMID:38030881][NCT:NCT07025226]

## Assessment questions

Question 1: Mechanisms of tumor recurrence. Which mechanism best explains how radiotherapy-induced senescent astrocytes can promote glioblastoma progression in experimental models? [PMID:34580063] A. Permanent elimination of neighboring glioma cells through p21 activation. B. Secretion of HGF that activates Met signaling in glioma cells. C. Suppression of all inflammatory cytokines within the irradiated brain. D. Direct inhibition of glioma cell migration through astrocyte-derived growth factors. Correct answer: B. Rationale: Radiation-induced senescent astrocytes secreted HGF, activating Met signaling and promoting glioma cell migration and invasion in experimental models. [PMID:34580063]

Question 2: Interpretation of preclinical senolytic evidence. Which statement accurately describes the evidence supporting cIAP2-targeted senolysis after radiotherapy in glioblastoma? [PMID:39972068] A. Birinapant has demonstrated improved overall survival in a randomized phase 3 glioblastoma trial. B. cIAP2 inhibition has been shown to prevent radiation-induced senescence in every normal brain cell population. C. Adjuvant birinapant eliminated senescent glioblastoma cells and prevented the emergence of recurrent tumors in preclinical mouse models. D. cIAP2-targeted therapy has established clinical efficacy regardless of tumor senescence status. Correct answer: C. Rationale: In patient-derived xenograft and immunocompetent mouse models, post-radiotherapy birinapant eliminated senescent glioblastoma cells and prevented recurrent tumor emergence, supporting preclinical rather than established clinical efficacy. [PMID:39972068]

Question 3: Clinical translation and patient selection. Which finding most directly supports the need to evaluate cellular heterogeneity before developing TMZ-associated senolytic treatment strategies? [PMID:41249587] A. TMZ pretreatment sensitized all tested glioblastoma models equally to DR5-mediated apoptosis. B. TMZ pretreatment sensitized U87MG but not T98G glioblastoma cells to DR5-mediated apoptosis, with sensitivity also observed in two of three primary patient-derived samples. C. Senescence induction consistently prevents all subsequent glioblastoma cell proliferation. D. Senolytic sensitivity is independent of differences in tumor-cell responses to TMZ. Correct answer: B. Rationale: Differential sensitization to DR5-mediated apoptosis across glioblastoma cell lines and primary samples demonstrates heterogeneous responses to TMZ-induced senescence and supports the need for patient-selection strategies. [PMID:41249587]
